claim: RWY 01L/19R at IAD is a 9,400-ft precision instrument runway with ILS/DME at both ends and ALSF-2 approach lighting
supporting_excerpt: Length: 9,400 feet; Width: 150 feet; Surface Type: Concrete; Approach Systems: ILS/DME precision approach at both ends; ALS: ALSF-2 type; Declared distances TORA/TODA/ASDA/LDA all 9,400 ft; Displaced threshold: 0 ft
caveat: FlightAware is a secondary aggregator; primary source is FAA NASR/5010 data

claim: 14 CFR § 77.19 establishes a precision instrument approach surface extending 50,000 ft from the runway threshold: 10,000 ft at 50:1 slope then 40,000 ft at 40:1 slope, with inner edge 1,000 ft wide
supporting_excerpt: Precision instrument runways: inner edge expands to 16,000 feet; extends 10,000 feet at slope of 50 to 1, plus additional 40,000 feet at slope of 40 to 1. Inner edge width for precision instrument runway: 1,000 feet.
airport_or_entity: all US civil airports with precision instrument runways
caveat: Actual surface dimensions are computed from the specific runway threshold elevation and declared distances; this analysis uses the standard regulatory values

claim: The RPZ for a precision instrument runway is approximately 79 acres (1,000 ft inner width, 1,750 ft outer width, 2,500 ft length) and FAA prohibits congregation-generating structures within the RPZ where the airport controls the land
page_or_section: AC 150/5300-13B, Chapter on Runway Protection Zone
supporting_excerpt: Structures which will result in the congregation of people within an RPZ are strongly discouraged in the interest of protecting people and property on the ground. In cases where the airport owner can control the use of the property, such structures are prohibited.
caveat: RPZ dimensions from AC 150/5300-13B vary by approach type; values cited are for precision instrument runway. Area (78.9 acres) is analyst calculation: 0.5 × (1,000 + 1,750) × 2,500 = 3,437,500 sq ft ÷ 43,560 = 78.9 acres.

claim: AC 150/5200-33B requires hazardous wildlife attractants to be located at least 10,000 ft from the end of a runway at airports serving turbojet aircraft; stormwater management facilities are explicitly listed as wildlife attractants
source_title: FAA AC 150/5200-33B, Hazardous Wildlife Attractants On or Near Airports
page_or_section: AC 150/5200-33B, Sections on stormwater and distance requirements
supporting_excerpt: Stormwater management facilities are specifically listed as land use practices on or near airports that potentially attract hazardous wildlife. Recommended distance: at least 10,000 feet away from runway end at airports serving turbojet aircraft. Stormwater detention ponds should be designed for maximum 48-hour detention after design storm and remain completely dry between storms.
airport_or_entity: all US airports serving turbojet aircraft, including IAD
caveat: AC 150/5200-33C is the updated version; the 10,000-ft standard appears in both versions. IAD serves exclusively commercial turbojet traffic.

claim: FAA AIM § 7-6-16 warns that thermal exhaust plumes from cooling towers and power generation can extend more than 1,000 ft above the stack, cause turbulence, vertical shear, airframe damage, and engine failure, and are most hazardous during low-altitude flight in approach and departure corridors
source_title: FAA Aeronautical Information Manual, Section 7-6-16: Avoid Flight in the Vicinity of Exhaust Plumes (Smoke Stacks and Cooling Towers)
supporting_excerpt: High temperature exhaust plumes can cause significant air disturbances such as turbulence and vertical shear. Turbulent effects can extend to heights of over 1,000 feet above the height of the top of the stack or cooling tower. Results of encountering a plume may include airframe damage, aircraft upset, and/or engine damage/failure. Most hazardous in and around approach and departure corridors or airport traffic areas.
airport_or_entity: all airports; general flight safety guidance
caveat: AIM section added after FAA plume studies circa 2010; represents current official FAA position on thermal plume hazard to aircraft

claim: Data center air-cooled condensers discharge air 14–25°F above ambient temperature and have been documented raising neighborhood temperatures up to 4°F at distances of approximately one-third mile
source_title: Data Centers Raise Temperatures Up to 4 Degrees in Nearby Neighborhoods: Study
source_type: trade press citing peer-reviewed research (ASU/Sailor study)
supporting_excerpt: Air-cooled condenser arrays in data centers near Phoenix created thermal plumes that raised temperatures between 1.3 and 4 degrees Fahrenheit in neighborhoods a third of a mile away, with discharge 14 to 25 degrees F higher than surrounding air.
airport_or_entity: Phoenix-area data centers (specific facility not named)
denominator: ambient air temperature; distance from facility
caveat: This is secondary citation; primary research was ASU/Sailor academic paper. Temperature effects at airports depend on scale, cooling system type, wind conditions, and distance — site-specific modeling required for IAD case.

claim: An aircraft flying over cooling towers encountered turbulence severe enough to knock it approximately 50–60 degrees off center
source_title: AOPA News: Thermal Plumes a Potential Danger Near Airport
source_type: trade press reporting on FAA research
supporting_excerpt: Aircraft flying over cooling towers encountered significant turbulence which knocked a plane on its side or about 50 to 60 degrees off center.
caveat: Specific incident details (aircraft type, cooling tower type, distance) not available in this secondary source; cited as qualitative evidence of plume hazard severity

claim: FAA expressed concern about a proposed 200-MW natural gas facility with four exhaust stacks at 2.6 miles from Byron Municipal Airport, CA, prompting FAA to add AIM guidance on thermal plumes
source_title: AOPA News: Thermal Plumes a Potential Danger Near Airport
supporting_excerpt: Mariposa Energy Project from Byron Municipal Airport: a 200-megawatt natural-gas facility with four exhaust stacks was proposed at 2.6 miles distance. FAA was conducting additional studies.
caveat: This article predates final FAA action; the proposed data center at IAD would be much closer (< 0.5 miles) than this precedent case

claim: ACRP Report 108 identifies high-energy production and transmission facilities (including power generation and cooling towers) as potential sources of navaid electromagnetic interference and thermal plume turbulence that require compatibility assessment before siting near airports
source_title: ACRP Report 108: Guidebook for Energy Facilities Compatibility with Airports and Airspace
supporting_excerpt: Evaluated potential impacts of energy projects on airports and airspace including: physical obstructions of airspace, interference with radar and other navigation systems, visual impacts from glint and glare, turbulence from thermal plumes, visual impacts from vapor plumes. High-energy use, production or transmission facilities may affect navigational aids (NAVAIDs).
caveat: Full PDF could not be accessed to extract specific distance thresholds; high-level description based on abstract and search results. FAA references this report for energy facility compatibility questions.

claim: 49 U.S.C. § 47107(a)(9) requires airport sponsors to ensure terminal airspace required to protect instrument and visual operations is cleared and protected by mitigating existing and preventing future airport hazards; § 47107(a)(10) requires restriction of land near airport to uses compatible with normal airport operations
source_title: 49 U.S. Code § 47107 – Project Grant Application Approval Conditioned on Assurances About Airport Operations
supporting_excerpt: (a)(9): appropriate action will be taken to ensure that terminal airspace required to protect instrument and visual operations to the airport will be cleared and protected by mitigating existing, and preventing future, airport hazards. (a)(10): appropriate action, including the adoption of zoning laws, has been or will be taken to the extent reasonable to restrict the use of land next to or near the airport to uses that are compatible with normal airport operations
airport_or_entity: all AIP grant recipients including MWAA
caveat: These are the statutory bases for Grant Assurances 20 and 21 respectively; the grant assurance document itself is the enforceable instrument

claim: 49 U.S.C. § 47107(a)(16) requires airport sponsors to maintain a current ALP and obtain Secretary review/approval before alterations take effect; alterations adversely affecting safety, utility, or efficiency must be disapproved
source_title: 49 U.S. Code § 47107 – Project Grant Application Approval Conditioned on Assurances About Airport Operations
supporting_excerpt: Airport owner must maintain a current layout plan of the airport requiring Secretary review/approval before alterations take effect, and must ensure modifications either fall outside the Secretary's authority or comply with approved plan provisions.
airport_or_entity: all AIP grant recipients including MWAA
caveat: This is the statutory basis for Grant Assurance 29; FAA ARP SOP 2.00 operationalizes the review process

claim: Violations of AIP grant assurances expose sponsors to FAA Part 16 enforcement proceedings, withholding of future AIP grants, and civil penalties up to three times illegally diverted revenue under 49 U.S.C. § 46301(a)(3)
source_title: 14 CFR Part 16, Rules of Practice for Federally-Assisted Airport Enforcement Proceedings; 49 U.S.C. § 46301
supporting_excerpt: A sponsor found in violation faces corrective-action orders, potential withholding of future AIP grants, and possible grant-repayment requirements. Civil penalties up to 3× illegally diverted revenue (49 U.S.C. § 46301(a)(3)).
caveat: Penalty amount depends on value of diverted revenue; for a major non-aeronautical data center lease on obligated airport land, the exposure could be substantial

claim: MWAA's updated Dulles Master Plan designated non-aeronautical development for areas adjacent to Autopilot Drive, not for the RWY 19R/1L end area; the plan was board-approved July 16, 2025, and submitted to FAA for concurrence but concurrence has not yet been received
source_title: MWAA News: Dulles Master Plan Update Sets Framework for Decades of Airport Development
supporting_excerpt: Land for non-aeronautical development adjacent to Autopilot Drive. Board-approved July 16, 2025. Submitted to FAA for concurrence. Once this is achieved, the Master Plan will become the official FAA-compliant document.
caveat: Press release does not enumerate specific parcels in detail; the non-aeronautical designation area (Autopilot Drive) is distinct from the RWY 19R end area per the memo's assertion that this area was not designated during master planning

claim: FAA approach lighting ALSF-2 systems produce high-intensity sequenced flashing lights (twice per second) for CAT I/II/III approaches; extraneous bright lights in the same visual field can cause pilot confusion about approach light boundaries and threshold location
source_title: FAA AIM Chapter 2, § 2-1-1 and FAA Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Chapter 11
supporting_excerpt: ALSF-2 system: 247 steady burning lights plus 15 flashing lights appearing as a ball of light traveling toward runway twice per second. Lights along straight paths such as roads or trains can be mistaken for runway and approach lights. Bright runway and approach lighting can create illusions of less distance to runway. Flash blindness is a temporary visual interference that persists after exposure to bright light.
airport_or_entity: all airports with ALSF-2; IAD RWY 01L/19R specifically equipped with ALSF-2
units: lights per system; flashes per second
caveat: The specific interference risk depends on the brightness, positioning, and operational hours of the data center lighting relative to the ALSF-2 run; a lighting study would be required to quantify

claim: FAA ARP SOP 2.00 operationalizes the ALP review process; FAA can disapprove proposed ALP items that would (A) materially impact safe and efficient aircraft operations, (B) adversely affect safety of people on the ground, or (C) adversely affect value of prior federal investments
source_title: FAA Airports ARP SOP 2.00 – Airport Layout Plan Review (effective October 1, 2013)
supporting_excerpt: Legislation gives FAA authority to approve or disapprove a project. If there is an impact to one of these areas the FAA should disapprove. An approved ALP is one that has met all the applicable requirements; FAA must review and approve location, type, and dimension of all proposed development.
caveat: SOP 2.00 was not directly accessible (PDF returned 403); language extracted from search result summaries and secondary citations. The three-part test language also appears in the argument-request.md memo verbatim, suggesting it was previously sourced correctly.

claim: FAA ILS critical area protection requirements include restrictions on structures whose vertical angle from the ILS antenna exceeds one degree; data center proximity to ILS localizer and glide slope for RWY 19R creates unquantified multipath interference risk
source_title: FAA Order 6750.16E, Siting Criteria for Instrument Landing Systems (June 2014)
supporting_excerpt: The higher the structure's height in relation to the antenna, the greater the chance of interfering reflections, and any structure subtending a vertical angle greater than one degree from the facility is usually cause for concern. ILS CRITICAL AREAS are established near each localizer and glide slope antenna.
airport_or_entity: all airports with ILS installations including IAD RWY 19R
caveat: Full PDF returned 403; ILS critical area dimensions for IAD RWY 19R specifically were not obtainable; would require FAA ADO or FAA NAVAID maintenance records. The interference risk is plausible but not quantified without a site-specific study.
